title: Lehman’s Legacy, ETF Performance & What Investors Still Get Wrong - Systematic Investor - Ep.366

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Lehman’s Legacy, ETF Performance & What Investors Still Get Wrong - Systematic Investor - Ep.366.docx

summary: Systematic Investor episode on institutional entry into managed futures, position sizing without leverage, why not to currency-convert prices, and the gap between fund and investor returns (YieldMax, Morningstar). Main conclusion: do not time in and out of strategies; use all data rather than a recent window, and hold trend following despite weak recent results.

coverage.note: Lehman analyst anecdote, Fed cut, institutions entering CTA
Fidelity managed futures paper, classic CTA deck
institutions timing, trend barometer and CTA/market numbers
positioning, bonds divergence, debt and Fed independence
UK vs Italy yields, cash-only position sizing question
do not currency convert, instrument significance, futures margin
crypto trend following, YieldMax article intro
investor underperformance numbers, active vs passive intro
allocation using all data vs recent window
Has the world changed? vol, significance, buy-and-hold default

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - first reader (80 claims) captured nearly all of the methodological content (sizing, FX conversion, window length, investor returns); misses are supporting data points, a few reasoning links, and one hosts' view on bond risk premia.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: initiates coverage of Lehman Brothers with an overweight recommendation that is iterated apparently on July 14th and August 27th
claims.claim: A sell-side overweight initiation on Lehman (reiterated until about 10 days before it failed) shows analyst buy ratings are poor risk signals near failures.

correction.issue: The precise details of the Morgan Stanley note (initiated 30 June, reiterated 14 July and 27 August) are given by Niels after he looked them up, not Rob; the lesson 'analyst buy ratings are poor risk signals near failures' is the first reader's inference, as the speakers only remark on the irony and the analyst's later career.
correction.fix: Niels notes that a Morgan Stanley note initiating Lehman at overweight on 30 June was reiterated on 14 July and 27 August, shortly before the September failure; the hosts treat it as an ironic anecdote, with no explicit methodological conclusion.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you're a hedge fund manager and you've lost a lot of money then then actually people are desperate to give you money
claims.claim: Allocators often give money to managers after large losses, opposite to how CTA allocation behaves, raising the question of whether to allocate after losses.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Christopher Waller who I think is one of the contenders to be the next Fed chair he did not descend
claims.claim: At the September 2025 25bp Fed cut, new governor Miran dissented for 50bp but contender Waller did not, and Powell dodged a question about Fed independence.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: some of these large institutions the black rocks the Fidelities have entered the CTA trend following space lately
claims.claim: Large managers such as BlackRock and Fidelity have entered trend-following products lately, suggesting growing institutional interest.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: managed future strategies represent one of the most time-tested researchbacked and structurally unique investment approaches available today
claims.claim: The Fidelity paper argues managed futures dynamically follow trends, keep low correlation to traditional assets and protect capital in crises, though not outperforming in every environment.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: when you put 10% of a 60/40 portfolio into into um trend it does better
claims.claim: The classic managed-futures case shows crisis episodes (GFC, 2022, 2000) and that adding 10% trend to a 60/40 portfolio improves mean, standard deviation, drawdown and Sharpe ratio.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: gatekeepers of huge model portfolios where um most likely they're going to be using their own products to give people exposure to trends
claims.claim: Big asset managers that run model portfolios will likely use their own trend products, creating new allocation flows to trend followers.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: It may be because you know trend hasn't done so well recently and who knows maybe this is buying the dip
claims.claim: The timing of institutional launches after weak trend performance may be dip-buying; Rob notes it is curious they did not launch 10-15 years ago.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we compared it to all the major hedge fund strategies um because we hadn't seen that being done before
claims.claim: Dawn Capital's paper compares evidence for trend following versus all major hedge fund strategies.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer finished yesterday at 41. So that's an improvement.
claims.claim: His trend barometer was at 41, an improvement over the previous 10 days but still not strong, with positions about 50-60% of typical risk.

correction.issue: The 50-60% of typical risk is Rob's own stated risk level (said in C05, 'equivalent numbers to you really'); Niels did not state a risk level in the transcript.
correction.fix: Niels' trend barometer was at 41, an improvement over about 10 days but still not strong; separately Rob says his own risk is about 50-60% of typical.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: such as equity, such as gold um have been really pulling uh the performance forward
claims.claim: CTA gains in recent months came from equity and gold trends.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: So CT index up 2.85 for the month, down only 3.62% for the year.
claims.claim: September 2025 CTA numbers: Beta 50 +2.43% in month, -0.45% YTD; CTA index +2.85% in month, -3.62% YTD; versus MSCI World +16.6% and S&P 500 TR +13.29% YTD.
claims.indicator: CTA indexes, MSCI World, S&P 500 TR

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it would be about 50 or 60% of my kind of typical kind of risk level
claims.claim: Rob runs about 50-60% of his typical risk because clear trends are lacking, with long equities, FX, bonds and short energy and Bitcoin.
claims.direction: long equities, FX, bonds; short energy, Bitcoin

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there's an awful lot of bad news out there that isn't to me priced in
claims.claim: Rob thinks rates markets underprice bad news such as Fed independence threats, yet his systematic book stays long bonds.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: carry is a much more significant factor in bond price movements than it is in equities
claims.claim: CTA bond positioning diverges because carry matters more for bonds than equities, so carry weight changes positions relative to trend.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: politicians in in in developed markets generally speaking get away with levels of debt that a few years ago people thought would be inconceivable
claims.claim: Bond market sell-offs on debt worries are the dog that has never barked; developed-market politicians get away with high debt (Truss was the exception).

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: at least in my systematic portfolio, I'm going to lose money
claims.claim: If discretionary views (Trump bad for bonds and equities) were right, a systematic long-bond portfolio would lose money, showing model and gut views can conflict.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So it can't just be a debt story. It must be an inflation story.
claims.claim: UK yields are above Italy's even though Italian debt/GDP is worse, so UK bond weakness reflects persistent inflation rather than debt alone.
claims.indicator: gilt vs BTP vs Bund spreads
claims.conditions: UK inflation persistently higher than EU

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So one is to kind of just effectively cut everything in half.
claims.claim: For cash-only (unlevered) portfolios where forecast-scaled positions exceed 100%, one option is to halve all positions so average exposure is 50% and maximum is 100%.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you're going to be going down from some say 25 to 12 a.5% which is a very low risk target
claims.claim: Halving works for high-volatility assets (e.g. EM stocks at 50% vol, giving a 25% target) but gives a risk target too low for liquid S&P 500 stocks.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you had instruments you were holding where you had less than the um, average forecast, then you'd have a smaller position in them
claims.claim: Alternative: cap forecasts at the average (10) instead of twice average (20), so weak forecasts shrink positions and cash creeps back in.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So in theory, yes, in practice, unless it was a big effect, I probably wouldn't bother because it would get get a bit too complicated.
claims.claim: Reallocating freed-up cash to other positions is theoretically optimal but usually not worth the complexity.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I would not combine those two things together. I tra trade them separately.
claims.claim: Do not currency-convert price series before trend following; trade the local-currency price and the FX rate as separate instruments.
claims.conditions: Applies to cash instruments and futures

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: removing the the potential for diversifying across two instruments, a currency and a stock market index
claims.claim: Combining the price and FX rate into one series removes diversification and increases correlation with a separate currency trade.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's quite hard to pick out statistically significant differences in performance of trend following of different instruments
claims.claim: Claims that trend following works better on some instruments than others usually lack statistical significance; checking 250 instruments will find a few significant by chance.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I just have to convert enough for the margin.
claims.claim: With futures only margin is converted, so FX exposure is a fraction of notional and the currency can be traded separately.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So um trend following on cryptocurrencies seems to work pretty well.
claims.claim: Trend following works well on cryptocurrencies by Rob's testing and by a crypto hedge fund he advises, with no guarantee for the future.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: An ETF gains 42% a year, its investors still lose money.
claims.claim: The YieldMax coin option income ETF earned 42% yet its investors lost money because of investor timing around its returns.
claims.indicator: fund percentage return vs investor cash return

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's going to be impossible for any individual um investor to actually earn the returns of a fund unless they literally buy and hold
claims.claim: Investor (cash/dollar-weighted) returns differ from fund (percentage) returns unless the investor buys and holds with no flows.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: lot of pe a lot more people are putting money in just before the thing goes down that are putting money in um when it's about to go
claims.claim: Investors pile in just before losses and leave before gains, so net flows turn a 42% fund return into a loss.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: $2.5 billion were coming in in net inflows. Yeah. But the investors lost a combined $ 35.5 million over the very same period
claims.claim: For the YieldMax fund, 2.5bn of net inflows and investors lost a combined 35.5m (about 1.5%) against a 42% fund gain.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: this is going to be more problematic in in funds whose returns are very let's say patchy or spiky
claims.claim: The return gap between fund and investor is larger for funds with strong positive or negative skew.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: But if you buying before one of those big losses you're going to on the back of what probably look like persistent gains in the past you're going to do very badly.
claims.claim: Trend following is positively skewed, option selling negatively skewed; flow-chasers buying after persistent gains in negative-skew strategies suffer the large losses.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: as a quant if you like you should say well this is generally true or is this just you know are the investors in this particular fund just uniquely stupid
claims.claim: When faced with an anecdote a quant should test whether it is generally true rather than extrapolate.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you look at the the whole universe of funds the underperformance is 1.7% a year
claims.claim: Morningstar finds investor returns trail fund returns by 1.7% a year across all US funds over 10 years, substantial over a decade.
claims.indicator: Morningstar investor return minus fund return

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there the underperformance is 4.4% 4% a year
claims.claim: The gap is worst in sector equity funds at 4.4% a year, likely because news and emotion (e.g. AI themes) drive buying after rallies.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: they're pretty poor at very poor at timing when to invest in things and when to take money out of things
claims.claim: Investors are poor at predicting the future and at timing entry into and exit from funds.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: one is that good managers continue to do well the other is that good managers is mean revert
claims.claim: Manager skill persistence can be tested through return autocorrelation: positive means good managers stay good, negative means mean reversion.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: any strategy that will go through long periods of underperformance or negative performance inevitably at some point people are going to be asking that question
claims.claim: Every strategy (CTAs, equity value) has long underperformance spells that provoke the 'has everything changed' question.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I want to use as much data as I possibly can. So, I'm just going to use all of my data and I'm going to treat it all equally.
claims.claim: The default allocator approach for blending trend with 60/40 is to use the full history (Rob's backtest runs back to 1970) with equal weight; a backfill trend index can be built by replication using futures prices.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you've done something that is not back testable because you have essentially created a an arbitrary point
claims.claim: Choosing to use only the last 2-3 years because trend did badly cannot be backtested; it smuggles in future information and would drive trend allocations to near zero.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you do look at things like persistence and autocorrelation of things like that, generally speaking, um the the effects aren't especially strong
claims.claim: Persistence and autocorrelation of strategy returns are weak, so there is no reliable conditioning variable to forecast CTA performance over the next 12 months.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there's a degradation of of out of sample performance as you reduce the size of the data you have available to you
claims.claim: Fitting on only 10, 5 or 3 years degrades out-of-sample results, nonlinearly: 50 years is good, 20-40 makes little difference, 2-3 is much worse.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: It doesn't make a lot of difference if you use 40 or even 30 years of data or even 20 years of data
claims.claim: Using 20-40 years of data performs about as well as 50, so the loss only appears with very short samples.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the world is always changing. And if you look at say the company that I work with, you know, we've been doing trend following for 51 years.
claims.claim: Trend following has survived 51 years of change because it adapts through research, though 1970s rules should not be applied unchanged.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: back in the 70s and the 80s it was you know more than 25% annual volatility. Today that index is less than 5% annualized volatility.
claims.claim: Lower CTA index returns reflect lower index volatility, from over 25% in the 1970s-80s to under 5% now, so returns should be lower.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in the earlier days when when there were fewer markets there was less diversification
claims.claim: Early trend-following results had fewer markets and less diversification, which complicates volatility-adjusted comparisons over time.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you still don't see a statistically significant difference in returns
claims.claim: Even if rolling trend returns degraded, the difference is not statistically significant, and with a low Sharpe strategy it could take another 50 years to know.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you're at the point where statistics can't really help you
claims.claim: Statistics cannot settle whether trend following has stopped working, so belief matters; the evidence on timing in and out of strategies is poor.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you should be buying and holding those funds or or strategies or risk factors unless you can prove very convincingly that you can do better
claims.claim: The default should be buy and hold of assets, funds, strategies or factors unless one can convincingly show timing adds value.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it didn't sound like from what I've read that PAL was lining up um you know complete um surrender and lots of rate cuts coming uh our way
claims.claim: After the 25bp September cut, Waller (a contender for Fed chair) did not dissent and Powell did not signal capitulation to a run of cuts, which the administration would not have wanted to see; the Fed is not pre-committed to many cuts.
claims.direction: fewer cuts than the administration wants
claims.testable: partly - FOMC votes and guidance are observable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the short-term traders index actually a good improvement 2.13% uh for the month down uh just 4.37% so far this year
claims.claim: September 2025 trend-index data beyond the CTA index: SG Trend up almost 4% in the month and down just over 4% YTD, and the short-term traders index up 2.13% in the month and down 4.37% YTD, i.e. managed futures recovering but still negative for the year.
claims.indicator: SG Trend index; short-term traders index
claims.conditions: Late 2025 rebound led by equities and gold trends

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the US aggregate bond index from S&P is up one and a quarter for the month, up 6 and a quarter for the year
claims.claim: Traditional assets kept delivering in 2025: the S&P US aggregate bond index was up 1.25% in September and 6.25% YTD, alongside equities, so a 60/40 benchmark outran trend indices.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: everybody getting into massive amount of debt, I think you could probably argue that many bond markets might uh you know probably should have a higher risk premier
claims.claim: Niels argues that, given large fiscal deficits and rising debt almost everywhere, many government bond markets should carry a higher risk premium than they currently do.
claims.indicator: bond term/risk premium versus debt levels
claims.testable: partly - term premium estimates exist but timing is not specified

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'm long bonds, but my risk is about half what is in equities
claims.claim: Rob's trend system holds a modest but persistent long bond position (BTPs, US 30-year, Canadian 10-year) with risk about half that on equities, so a bond sell-off driven by Fed-independence or inflation fears would cost his systematic book money.
claims.indicator: bond trend signal (with carry) and risk allocation
claims.conditions: Trend and carry signals still long
claims.testable: yes - positions follow a rules-based system

claims.speaker: unclear (Rob Carver or Niels Kaastrup-Larsen)
claims.quote: in the UK we did hit 27year high yields uh only a couple of weeks ago higher than windless trust
claims.claim: UK gilt yields recently reached 27-year highs, above the Truss-crisis peak, together with inflation that stayed high since 2022 while EU inflation mean-reverted, a case where bond markets have priced debt and inflation concerns.
claims.testable: yes - gilt yield history is public

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So if my forecasts become really weak, then yes, I will cut my position, but if they get stronger than average, then I can't really do anything about it.
claims.claim: In an unlevered account forecast scaling is asymmetric: weak forecasts can shrink positions but stronger-than-average ones cannot raise them, so the fraction of the forecast-strength information that is used falls.
claims.conditions: Cash-only portfolios with a 100% notional cap
claims.testable: yes - compare capped versus uncapped forecasts in a backtest

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Because it would have had a sort of systematic drift added to it, which is the depre depreciation of the currency effect on top of it.
claims.claim: Converting a foreign asset's price into home currency before trend following adds the exchange-rate trend to the asset's trend (e.g. a falling pound makes a US ETF look stronger), so the signal becomes a blend of two instruments rather than a clean trend in either.
claims.indicator: home-currency price of a foreign-listed asset
claims.direction: trend signal inflated when home currency depreciates
claims.testable: yes - compare signals on converted versus local price series

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: he looks at the the um the annual reports and the kind of cash movements um and looks at the the net flows in and out
claims.claim: Investor (cash/dollar-weighted) return for a fund can be estimated from its annual reports and net flows in and out, then compared with the headline percentage return; the flow-weighted aggregate is what investors actually earned.
claims.indicator: fund net flows; investor return minus fund return
claims.conditions: Needs fund-level flow and NAV data
claims.testable: yes - Morningstar-type calculation on fund flows

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: There's probably no skill here. It probably just that by luck, you know, there are so many funds out there that
claims.claim: In the few funds where investors beat the fund's own return, the cause is probably luck rather than timing skill, given so many funds; the industry average gap is negative.
claims.testable: yes - test cross-sectional dispersion against chance

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the percentage of of um assets that are passively managed or in managed by indices has just just kind of gone up um persistently over quite long period of time now
claims.claim: The share of assets in passive or index strategies has risen persistently over a long period, so the passive-versus-active debate is largely won by passive.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the FT sort of said well this is a very poor analysis but actually ultimately um it doesn't really kind of settle the argument one way or the other
claims.claim: Evidence on whether active-manager performance persists (the persistence scorecard debate) is unsettled; a critique of the scorecard analysis does not settle the question either way.
claims.testable: partly - persistence tests exist but results are disputed

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: just over time markets get more efficient and therefore there's less alpha to be collected
claims.claim: Plausible 'the world has changed' stories for weak CTA returns (Trump policy, more algorithmic trading, markets becoming more efficient so less alpha) are narratives that cannot be separated from bad luck without a testable method.
claims.testable: partly - test for structural break in trend returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Even ignoring trading costs, you know, you're just going to have mostly noise.
claims.claim: An allocation optimised on a very short window (e.g. the last 10 days) is mostly noise and would also cause constant switching and trading costs, showing that out-of-sample quality degrades as the fit window shrinks.
claims.testable: yes - compare out-of-sample results by window length
